content: In July 2021, the first modular update on hepatitis C self-testing guidelines was introduced. This update marked the second modular revision focusing on hepatitis C testing and treatment. By 2023, all updates will be consolidated with existing recommendations into a single comprehensive guideline addressing the prevention, testing, care, and treatment of hepatitis B and C, encompassing all relevant guidance. Five systematic reviews and meta-analyses were conducted to address key research questions. Additionally, four surveys on values and preferences were carried out to assess the perspectives of affected communities and healthcare workers. Cost-effectiveness analyses and case studies on implementation experiences were also included to inform the formulation of recommendations. Key Areas of New Recommendations: 1. Treatment in Adolescents and Children: The 2018 treat all recommendation for adults has been expanded to include all adolescents and children aged three years or older with chronic hepatitis C infection. The same pangenotypic direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens recommended for adults (sofosbuvir/daclatasvir, sofosbuvir/velpatasvir, glecaprevir/pibrentasvir) are now recommended for these younger populations. 2. Simplified Service Delivery: Expansion of hepatitis C testing and treatment services through decentralization to lower-level facilities, ideally at the same site. Integration with existing services such as primary care, harm reduction programs, prisons, and HIV services. Promotion of task-sharing by enabling trained non-specialist doctors and nurses to deliver hepatitis C testing, care, and treatment. 3. HCV RNA Testing: Point-of-care (PoC) HCV RNA assays are now recommended as an additional approach to diagnose viremic infection, particularly in marginalized populations such as people who inject drugs and hard-to-reach communities with limited healthcare access and high rates of loss to follow-up. Reflex HCV RNA testing for individuals with a positive HCV antibody result is recommended to enhance linkage to care and treatment. This can be achieved through laboratory-based reflex testing using pre-collected specimens or clinic-based reflex testing with immediate specimen collection following a positive rapid HCV antibody test result, avoiding the need for a second visit. Recommendations for DAA Treatment: Who to Treat? Treatment using pangenotypic DAA regimens is recommended for all adults, adolescents, and children aged three years and above with chronic hepatitis C infection, regardless of disease stage. Adults (≥18 years): Strong recommendation; moderate certainty of evidence. Adolescents (12–17 years): Strong recommendation; moderate/low certainty of evidence. Older children (6–11 years): Strong recommendation; moderate/very low certainty of evidence. Younger children (3–5 years): Conditional recommendation; very low certainty of evidence. What DAA Regimens to Use? Sofosbuvir/Daclatasvir (SOF/DCV) for 12 weeks: High certainty of evidence for adults and adolescents; very low certainty for younger children. Sofosbuvir/Velpatasvir (SOF/VEL) for 12 weeks: High certainty for adults; low certainty for adolescents and older children; very low certainty for younger children. Glecaprevir/Pibrentasvir (G/P) for eight weeks: High certainty for adults; moderate certainty for adolescents and older children; very low certainty for younger children. Simplified Service Delivery: 1. Decentralization: Delivery of HCV testing and treatment at peripheral health or community-based facilities, ideally at the same site, is recommended to increase access to diagnosis, care, and treatment. These facilities may include primary care centers, harm reduction sites, prisons, HIV/ART clinics, community-based organizations, and outreach services. (Strong recommendation; moderate certainty of evidence for people who inject drugs and prisoners; low certainty for the general population and people living with HIV.) 2. Integration: Integration of HCV testing and treatment with existing care services at peripheral health facilities is recommended. These services may include primary care, harm reduction programs (e.g., needle and syringe programs, opioid agonist maintenance therapy sites), prisons, and HIV/ART services. (Strong recommendation; moderate certainty of evidence for people who inject drugs and prisoners; low certainty for the general population and people living with HIV.) 3. Task Sharing: Delivery of HCV testing, care, and treatment by trained non-specialist doctors and nurses is recommended to expand access to diagnosis, care, and treatment. (Strong recommendation; moderate certainty of evidence.) HCV RNA Testing for Diagnosis and Treatment Response: 1. Laboratory-Based HCV NAT Testing: Following a positive HCV antibody serological test result, quantitative or qualitative nucleic acid testing (NAT) for HCV RNA is recommended as the preferred strategy to diagnose viremic infection. (Strong recommendation; moderate/low certainty of evidence.) 2. HCV Core Antigen Assay: An assay to detect HCV core antigen (p22), with comparable clinical sensitivity to laboratory-based HCV RNA NAT assays, can be an alternative approach to diagnose HCV viremic infection. (Conditional recommendation; moderate certainty of evidence.) 3. Point-of-Care HCV RNA Assays: The use of HCV point-of-care (PoC) viral load NAT assays can be an alternative to laboratory-based HCV RNA NAT assays for diagnosing HCV viremic infection. (Conditional recommendation; low/moderate certainty of evidence.) 4. Reflex HCV RNA Testing: Reflex HCV RNA testing in individuals with a positive HCV antibody test result is recommended as a key strategy to promote linkage to care and treatment. This can be implemented through laboratory-based reflex testing using pre-collected specimens or clinic-based reflex testing with immediate specimen collection following a positive rapid HCV antibody test result. (Conditional recommendation; low quality of evidence.) Use of Dried Blood Spot (DBS) Specimens: DBS specimens have been validated by assay manufacturers for serological and virological testing under various storage and transport conditions. Manufacturer protocols now describe procedures for DBS and plasma separation card (PSC) specimen collection, processing, transportation, and analysis. DBS specimens may be considered for HBsAg and HCV antibody serology testing in settings where venous blood collection is not feasible, rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) are unavailable, or individuals have poor venous access (e.g., in drug treatment programs or prisons). (Conditional recommendation; moderate certainty for HBV, low certainty for HCV.) DBS specimens may also be considered for testing HBV DNA and HCV RNA for diagnosing viremia in settings with limited access to laboratory facilities or timely specimen delivery. (Conditional recommendation; low certainty for HBV, moderate certainty for HCV.) Updated WHO Consolidated Guidelines: The updated WHO Consolidated Guidelines on HIV, viral hepatitis, and sexually transmitted infections (STIs) for key populations will be published in July 2022. These guidelines outline a public health response for five key populations: men who have sex with men, sex workers, people in prisons and other closed settings, people who inject drugs, and transgender and gender-diverse individuals. New recommendations include the use of peer navigators to support key populations in starting and adhering to treatment and offering online delivery of services while ensuring data security and confidentiality. Good practice statements on chemsex and behavioral interventions are also included. For HCV testing and treatment, the guidelines recommend: Offering 3–6 monthly testing for HCV viremia in individuals at ongoing risk or with a history of treatment-induced or spontaneous clearance of HCV infection. (Conditional recommendation; very low certainty of evidence.) Offering pangenotypic DAA-HCV treatment without delay to individuals with recently acquired HCV infection and ongoing risk. Objectives of the Updated HCV Guidelines: The updated guidelines aim to provide evidence-based recommendations on key HCV-related topics identified in the 2018 WHO Guidelines for the care and treatment of persons diagnosed with chronic HCV infection and the 2017 WHO Guidelines on hepatitis B and C testing. The three priority areas are: 1. Use of direct-acting antiviral (DAA) treatment for adolescents and children aged ≥3 years. 2. Simplified service delivery (decentralization, integration, and task sharing). 3. HCV diagnostics – use of PoC HCV RNA viral load and reflex HCV RNA viral load testing. These updates align with the modular approach adopted since 2020 in response to emerging evidence on hepatitis B and C virus infections.
